# MASTER EXECUTION PLAN — 1,296-Opportunity Online Income Portfolio

**Version:** 1.0 — 13 October 2026  
**Repository:** [`Hi62384/Proj`](https://github.com/Hi62384/Proj)  
**Repository baseline reviewed:** `fac644ff47b614bf650d5acee8649afb794ad889` (`main`)  
**Currency:** Canadian dollars unless explicitly stated otherwise  
**Status:** EXECUTION PLAN ONLY. **No businesses, accounts, websites, sales, customer conversations, or payment systems have been created by this plan.**

> **MISSION:** Search across *every legitimate niche* in the repository without bias toward Godot, gaming, software, trades, professional services, or any existing personal project. Seek the fastest credible real revenue; build repeatable offerings; automate the proven operations; diversify as actual buyer evidence permits. Cover all 1,296 catalogue records as candidate opportunities. **Do not interpret “all opportunities” as permission to launch 1,296 products at once.** Every idea enters a measured decision funnel. Unvalidated ideas are not business assets and cannot legitimately be assigned forecast earnings.

## How to use this document

This is both the **operating manual for the portfolio** and a **per-opportunity activation index**. Start with Sections 0–8 and the first 72-hour checklist. Use the model playbook matching an offer's mode in Section 13, consult the industry-specific cautions in Section 14, then locate its exact ID in Appendix A (expanded niches) or Appendix B (114 earlier opportunities). Keep the original `Opportunity_Atlas.html` open as the searchable interface; this Markdown file supplies the execution steps. Return to the stop/scale gates before allocating additional time or money.

## 0. Reality, scope, and operating covenant

**Do not start by automating 1,296 businesses.** There are **197 expanded industry slices × six ideas each = 1,182** newly scoped hypotheses, plus **54** opportunities from the original research and **60** from the earlier fast-cash study. The 114 earlier records contain **18 pairs previously marked equivalent**, so the raw number is deliberately *not* a count of 1,296 independent validated markets. Many expanded ideas share the same business mechanism; a generic calculator adapted to 40 trades is not 40 proven revenue streams. Source references show a paid category, platform capability, or competitor—not that one specific offer will sell.

A portfolio can eventually contain many revenue streams, but the constraints are **acquisition**, **real customer value**, **support**, **human time**, **quality**, **privacy**, and **cash settlement**. Designing hundreds of unvisited storefronts is not a revenue strategy. Broad *research* is cheap; broad *operating obligations* are expensive. The implementation system must be capable of *considering* all opportunities while funding, launching and supporting only those that meet gates.

**Non-negotiable rules:**

1. No industry receives an automatic bonus for being related to the user's projects, previous prompts, or technical preferences. Skill and delivery competence are assessed separately as real costs, never confused with demand.
2. Track initial revenue, settled cash, monthly operating profit, and profit **after valuing every owner hour**. Do not equate any of them.
3. Do not guarantee customers, marketplace visibility, returns, or payouts. Time-to-first-sale ranges describe possibilities and always include the possibility of **never selling**.
4. Do not offer medical diagnosis, legal advice, regulated financial advice, safety certification, deceptive compliance guarantees, unauthorized security tests, or unlicensed creative material.
5. Use explicit buying intent, opted-in research participants, authorized marketplace interactions, and partner relationships; avoid mass unsolicited messages, fake proof, unauthorized scraping, hidden upsells, and terms-of-service violations.
6. A payment account and tax obligations require accurate onboarding by an authorized person. Never store secrets, consumer records, or personal credentials in this public research repository.
7. Human review is mandatory for irreversible actions, claims of legal/medical/safety correctness, payments and refunds outside approved limits, customer-facing messages without permission, and production writes to third-party accounts.
8. Keep a log of every decision: opportunity ID, buyer signal, experiment, spend, delivery hours, evidence, gate and next review date.
9. Pause or shut down losing experiments; honoring existing purchasers' lawful support/refund commitments takes precedence over starting more ideas.
10. In the first month, favor short acquisition loops over abstract automation. In month three and beyond, favor repeatable net contribution per total owner hour over the *number* of nominal income streams.

**Definitions:** A *hypothesis* is an offer with no paid evidence. A *validated pilot* has a real paying customer and an accepted outcome; one sale alone is not repeatable demand. A *repeatable line* has at least two independent paid orders or credible paid renewal behavior, documented acquisition, and positive unit contribution. A *mostly automated line* has measured end-to-end manual workload including sales, onboarding, support, releases, and incidents—not merely “automatic file downloads.”

## 2. Portfolio design: broad discovery, narrow execution

Run three interconnected work queues rather than 1,296 parallel companies.

**Queue A — Market radar (breadth):** Every 7 days evaluate a rotating selection of 10–20 ideas drawn from at least five unrelated sectors. Check current buyer requests, the pricing of existing products, data-access feasibility, fulfillment burden, restrictions, and whether any buyer can be reached ethically. Entry is cheap. Producing a catalogue entry or an AI-generated mockup is **not** a launch.

**Queue B — Paid validation (speed):** Carry up to **three separately scoped offers** in outreach at one time, from at least two different sectors. Keep at most **one active delivery commitment** until the first product/service is accepted. Do not send more messages than you can answer promptly. You may test a one-time product and a recurring product together only when the cash and labor budget allow.

**Queue C — Operating businesses (quality):** Admit a product only after a paid gate and verified cost of delivery. Initially cap at **three operational business lines**, ideally with at least two different customer segments; the precise number is a capacity constraint, not a diversity quota. Lines can share a codebase without sharing customer files or revenue accounting. A new storefront for a new sector is not automatically a new business.

### Why this balances speed and “passive” income

- Fast fixed-scope work can produce initial cash because the buyer has a current problem, but cannot be called passive while a human is delivering every order.
- Paid digital downloads and licensed assets can deliver automatically but still need a discovery channel, legal rights, support and updates.
- Recurring monitoring, narrow integrations and APIs can be more valuable over time but require reliability, security, ongoing customer trust and churn control.
- Content, directories and marketplaces can become assets *after* distribution is solved; they generally do not belong in the first-week primary path.

**Capital allocation by maturity:** spend money finding and serving a specific paying buyer before spending it on generic infrastructure. Once customers repeatedly purchase one problem class, create a shared adapter or downloadable product. When multiple customers pay for the same repeated workflow, consider a subscription or usage API. Sell complementary products to buyers who actually want them; never assume every cross-sell converts.

### Operating cadence at a 20-hour/week starting capacity

| Workstream | Initial weekly allocation | Later target |
|---|---:|---:|
| Prospect research + qualification | 5 hours | 3 hours + automated *research only* |
| Buyer conversations + compliant offers | 5 hours | 3 hours + partner referrals |
| Paid delivery and acceptance | 6 hours | 4 hours + reusable workflow |
| Product/code/asset development | 2 hours | 5 hours funded by paid evidence |
| Finances, quality, privacy, maintenance | 2 hours | 5 hours as complexity grows |

The hours are an editable capacity policy, **not** a claim that any of those tasks have already been performed. If 20 hours per week proves insufficient, reduce parallelism, avoid promising fast delivery, or stop expansion. A 10-hour week roughly halves the available validation and fulfillment capacity; a 40-hour week should not encourage unbounded commitments.

## 3. Prioritization and opportunity-state machine

### A. Initial filter (must pass all)

- A named buyer, a specific expensive/repetitive problem, and a credible way to contact that buyer legally.
- Realistically deliverable MVP with existing skills or affordable approved expertise.
- Outcome can be objectively accepted (matching record counts, a working report, usable template, functioning authorized alert, etc.).
- No unverified rights to private datasets or copyrighted assets, and no regulated professional judgment automated without safeguards.
- Price and delivery hours plausibly leave positive contribution after platform, payment, FX, support, refunds, and acquisition.
- There is at least one independent demand signal specific to the task, not merely “people buy software.”

### B. Weighted scoring, deliberately niche-neutral

For any candidate that passes the gate, score each axis 0–5 and calculate:

`Priority = 7×Speed + 5×Profit + 4×Automation + 2×Evidence/Acquisition + 2×Scalability` (maximum 100).

This exactly implements **35/25/20/10/10**. Require a written reason and source for each dimension. Speed means *credible time to acquire a buyer*, not time to publish a landing page. Profit uses projected *net contribution after all cash costs and reasonable owner time*, not fantasy gross sales. Automation includes onboarding, acquisition, support, exceptions and incidents. Evidence requires recent category spending **and**, at the high end, actual exact-offer paid transactions. Scalability means support hours and customer acquisition need not grow linearly.

**Tie-breakers:** documented buyer requests; lower sales friction; smaller refundable paid pilot; fewer data/rights constraints; greater margin per total human hour; lower irreversible commitments. If a `regulated` risk flag exists, require a separate compliance review and favor a less sensitive experiment, unless you actually possess authorized expertise and a buyer relationship.

**No personal-interest score.** Experience can reduce estimated development time, but **cannot stand in for customer willingness to pay**. A warehouse report can beat a game plugin; a game plugin can beat an agency service if real purchases support it. Data decides.

### C. Measured evidence changes priority

Record 10 candidate buyer signals, then up to three sales offers. After each batch replace predictions with observed values: qualified conversations, proposals, paid orders, acquisition hours, net revenue per sale, support hours, and refund/chargeback causes. A low initial score can leap to first place when a buyer pays. A 90-point hypothetical must fall behind a 70-point offer with clear profitable paid demand. Do not turn a “0.05 conversion prior” into a claimed 5% probability of success.

### D. State machine (all opportunities move through this)

`IN_CATALOGUE → DESK_SCREENED → BUYER_EVIDENCE → OFFER_DRAFTED → REAL_BUYER_TEST → PAID_PILOT → ACCEPTED_DELIVERY → REPEATABLE → AUTOMATION_CANDIDATE → OPERATING → SCALING`.

Any active state may transition to `PAUSED`, `NEEDS_LEGAL_REVIEW`, `NEEDS_CUSTOMER_ACCESS`, `NOT_ECONOMIC`, or `RETIRED`. Retired does not mean all contractual obligations vanish. Each transition requires a dated note, evidence URL or permitted internal record, budget used, hours invested, next-review date, and an explicit human approver. **No pipeline stage is advanced by AI saying “looks promising.”**

### E. Test allocation method

Use a bounded *explore/exploit* policy: reserve roughly 70% of launch time for the best evidenced active opportunity, 20% for one cross-sector challenger, and 10% for breadth research/documentation. In week one, when none has actual sales, split experiment design more evenly but still limit delivery to one job. Each week surface ideas from an industry not currently in the active pipeline to prevent blind spots. Only switch based on comparable buyer evidence, not novelty.

## 4. Exact 72-hour implementation sprint

**North-star output:** an objectively scoped, publicly honest offer presented through authorized channels to real potential buyers, with an attempt to obtain one paid order. A paid outcome is a stretch target, not an assumption. If there is no buyer, get concrete rejection reasons at the lowest feasible cost.

| Window | Work | Required deliverable | Stop/decision |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hours 0–2 | Open atlas and filter Fast-cash (F) across unrelated sectors; exclude regulated/unauthorized work and implausible delivery. | 20-candidate worksheet: ID, buyer, problem, competitive substitute, channel, time. | No idea advances solely for high heuristic score. |
| Hours 2–4 | Compare 20 candidates, inspect actual comparable products and dated buyer requests; select three offers in at least three sectors. | Three one-page business hypotheses, each with visible buyer path. | If no real buyer route, replace candidate. |
| Hours 4–7 | Check access, platform rules, business onboarding and Canadian communication rules. | Written permission/terms checklist and data safety plan. | Don't message or handle data until authorized. |
| Hours 7–12 | Produce **one small honest sample per offer** using synthetic/permitted data. Examples: reconciled SKU exception CSV, invoice mapping sample, vendor quote comparison. | Before/after demonstration plus reproducible acceptance test. | If sample is unreliable or requires unqualified professional judgment, stop. |
| Hours 12–16 | Draft clear price, in-scope/out-of-scope, revisions, turnaround *after accepted inputs and funded milestone*, refunds/remedy, and customer responsibility. | Three buyer-ready offers with delivery-hour estimate. | Don't promise indefinite SLA, results or a capability not built. |
| Hours 16–24 | Locate 5–10 relevant explicit requests or consenting introductions; respond individually within channel terms. | CRM rows: buyer request, offer ID, permission basis, reply, next step, time spent. | Do not auto-send unsolicited commercial electronic messages. |
| Hours 24–36 | Hold discovery conversations. Ask for redacted samples or sandbox credentials **only through approved secure paths**. | Buyer baseline, current method, acceptance criteria, actual urgency and budget objection. | If problem solved for free by existing tool, do not invent differentiation. |
| Hours 36–48 | Ask suitable prospects for a paid scoped pilot with verified payment channel or funded marketplace milestone. | A paid commitment, an explicit decline, or substantive buyer objection. | No actual paid customer = no claim of product-market fit. |
| Hours 48–60 | If funded, deliver the first bounded task; otherwise revise one offer or sector based on responses. | Accepted file/report or a revised outreach hypothesis. | Avoid building speculative hosted infrastructure. |
| Hours 60–72 | Reconcile fees, delivery/support/acquisition hours, and decision evidence; choose the next seven-day focus. | Go/narrow/pivot/stop decision and actuals ledger. | A proposed sale is not settled cash. |

**Example cross-sector test trio — conditional on actual visible requests:** `EXP-022-01` warehouse inventory reconciliation, `EXP-032-01` event-venue quote cleanup, and `EXP-129-01` SEO Search Console export cleanup. They illustrate distinct buyers, not universal winners. Replace any one of them with a better-documented opportunity from the 20-candidate queue. The optional `FAST-O01` reporting sprint is just one alternative; do **not** make it the permanent focus.

**No-sales response:** zero conversions after five relevant requests proves little. Diagnose whether buyers could be reached, whether the demonstrated benefit matters, the competitive substitute, pricing, and actual delivery risk. After a deliberate 30–40 qualified-prospect test with meaningful revisions, retire or move to a different buyer problem; never escalate ad spend simply to defend the original idea.

## 5. Daily action calendar: days 1–30

This calendar assumes **20 hours/week** and that a first paid task may *not* appear. It does not override a customer's contractual deadline. On weeks with paying work, replace experimentation with delivery rather than double-booking hours. Each day's main task ends in evidence or an artifact—not a vague “work on business.”

| Day | Concrete action | Required observable result | Decision trigger |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 1 | Build a 20-offer comparison from **at least five nonadjacent sectors**. Check legal and buyer-access blockers; shortlist three. | Three ID-linked offer briefs, sources, and a capacity estimate. | Reject unqualified/sensitive work. |
| 2 | Build one honest ten-row or single-workflow demo for each of the three. Inspect current competitors, not only their prices. | Three repeatable proof samples and acceptance tests. | No paid offers for untested or rights-unclear deliverables. |
| 3 | Respond to five strong explicit requests or permissioned introductions; ask a concrete discovery question. | Actual inquiry/response log with permitted contact basis. | If there is no identifiable buyer path, rotate one sector. |
| 4 | Follow up *where permitted* and inspect redacted sample(s). Offer a funded, bounded pilot. | One or more real quotes with sample-dependent scope. | If no qualified conversations, fix channel specificity first. |
| 5 | Deliver the first paid pilot if secured; otherwise interview/demonstrate to three prospects. | Accepted output or specific buyer objections. | Never fabricate completed-client proof. |
| 6 | Reconcile errors, invoice terms, time spent, and customer acceptance; request an honest testimonial only if earned and permitted. | Quality checklist, ledger row, customer feedback. | Redesign scope if human work exceeds ceiling. |
| 7 | Weekly gate: compare actual purchase interest and owner-hour economics across all three offers. | One chosen lead offer, one challenger, one paused idea. | Stop unproductive extra builds. |
| 8 | Revise the best offer's promise and show sample to two additional buyers. | Revised scope/pricing grounded in objections. | Do not cut price without changing scope or evidence. |
| 9 | Create a clean data-intake template, sample validation script and delivery naming convention for the lead offer. | Documented intake and fixture-based test. | No production data in public repo. |
| 10 | Test the same offer in a second *permitted* channel (e.g. marketplace request versus warm referral). | Channel-labelled qualified conversations. | Do not spray identical messages across sites. |
| 11 | Attempt second paid delivery or measure why first buyer did not return. | Sale, specific refusal, or repeat-use signal. | No subscription without an ongoing problem. |
| 12 | Reduce top two repeated delivery steps; measure before/after time. | Saved script/template with tests and rollback notes. | No automation of unclear judgment. |
| 13 | Test a low-touch downloadable alternative with three actual potential buyers, preferably another sector. | One paid/declined pre-sale decision, not a 40-page sales site. | Do not build a content library before paid proof. |
| 14 | Two-week review: sum spend, settled cash, gross margin, acquisition and owner hours. | Continue/pivot/stop on both tracks. | If no buyer evidence, move to a new problem. |
| 15 | Draft a versioned, reusable implementation SOP for the winning service or product. | Accepted inputs/outputs and error handling. | Do not promise client-specific infinite customization. |
| 16 | Check eligible checkout/storefront providers, refund rules, identity requirements, taxes and country restrictions. | Eligibility/terms checklist, *not* a fabricated live account. | Stop if seller/product is not permitted. |
| 17 | Set up a minimal paid product/offer page if validated; otherwise improve request-specific proposal clarity. | Working public listing **only if approved**, or prepared copy. | A landing page is not a sale. |
| 18 | Build unit/regression tests for the existing deliverable and test failure inputs. | Passing tests with known unsupported cases. | Fail closed on unknown mappings and high-risk data. |
| 19 | Repeat a small buyer-intent search in two sectors missing from the initial week. | Five new qualified problem observations. | Keep niche neutrality. |
| 20 | Trial an agency or implementation partner on a bounded paid referral arrangement, where allowed. | Written partner criteria and one real conversation. | No referral payment that violates professional rules. |
| 21 | Three-week review: support backlog, quality, actual customer acquisition and continuing cash. | Evidence-based decision on second operational line. | Only add a line with capacity and obligations covered. |
| 22 | If at least three paid repeatable cases exist, extract nonconfidential common code or reusable licensed template. | Versioned package and provenance audit. | Otherwise keep improving service delivery. |
| 23 | Test whether customers will pay for support/care beyond initial work; define exact recurring value. | Paid commitment or explicit refusal. | “Subscription” is not justified by billing convenience. |
| 24 | Formalize support inbox, issue categories, expected response boundary and refund/remedy process. | SOP with escalation owners and contact paths. | No fake 24/7 human support. |
| 25 | Add one automated failure notification and one ledger reconciliation test. | Demonstrated failed-run alert and verified transaction totals. | No automatic irreversible live action. |
| 26 | Run a second cross-sector offer test that uses existing infrastructure but genuinely different buyers. | One concrete buyer-specific offer and channel. | Stop if shared infrastructure hides high custom-work cost. |
| 27 | Evaluate paid ads **only if** first-order contribution and landing page conversion are measured. | Written capped test budget or explicit decision not to advertise. | Zero evidence = zero scale spend. |
| 28 | Calculate actual realized CAD profit after fees, FX, refunds, expenses and owner time. | Actuals-versus-forecast table. | Do not count model revenue as reality. |
| 29 | Identify one repetitive task to document/delegate only if safe and financially justified. | SOP with objective quality check and maximum spend. | No contractor access to entire client account by default. |
| 30 | Hold the first portfolio review: choose one scale candidate, one small challenger, and the next sectors to screen. | 60-day backlog, WIP cap, cash buffer, and scored decisions. | No forced launch quota. |

**Daily minimum record:** date, `opportunity_id`, channel/source, status, exact problem, buyer consent/terms status, minutes, cash spend, actual paid dollars, refund exposure, outcome and next task. **Weekly minimum record:** qualified leads, proposals, paid conversions, owner hours, settled cash, active contracts, defect count, churn, and best new sector discovered.

## 6. Weekly and monthly rollout: day 31 to month 24

### Days 31–60: create the first repeatable product line

| Period | Acquisition | Product and infrastructure | Proof required to proceed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Week 5 | Revisit buyer objections and narrow targeting; ask existing customers for permitted introductions. | Make delivery reproducible: config, fixtures, verification, versioned files, run logs. | A second independent paid transaction or genuine renewal; positive contribution. |
| Week 6 | Run one different-sector challenger test; avoid launching ten versions. | Add idempotent intake and failure escalation; use hosted checkout or marketplace payments. | Customer can receive a correct output without manual copying, with human exception path. |
| Week 7 | Seek a partner with existing buyer access; test one referral agreement. | Make cancellations, refunds, opt-out and data deletion operational; restrict permissions. | No unresolved major service incident. |
| Week 8 | Review acquisition conversion and time by channel; cut the weakest. | Build the first productized template/adapter **only if customer outputs repeat**. | Contribution/hour improves; not merely percentage “automated.” |

### Days 61–90: make automation reliable, not just impressive

| Period | Action | Measurable exit criterion |
|---|---|---|
| Week 9 | Offer a bounded paid recurring test to a customer who demonstrably needs ongoing service. | Scope, volume limits, cancellation terms, success measure, owner approval. |
| Week 10 | Add secure event logging, scheduled health checks and reconciliation. | Simulate delivery error and notice it within the defined internal monitoring window. |
| Week 11 | Compare new cross-industry offers against the winner using real conversion and support data. | A documented decision: replicate adapter, specialize, or stay focused. |
| Week 12 | Build one self-service alternative, licensed pack or connector based on paid learning. | At least a real paid trial or a reason to stop before a large release. |
| Week 13 | Quarterly economic review and data-rights audit. | Monthly operating and economic profit, MRR, churn, payout pipeline, workload, next 90-day plan. |

**WIP rule through day 90:** at most three *supported* lines, one major feature release at a time, and no live feature without a support/rollback owner. An external customer's urgent issue outranks a new speculative niche. “Get many businesses running” does not authorize unmeasured vendor charges or unsigned access to customer systems.

### Months 4–12: measured multi-niche expansion

| Month | Portfolio build-out | Distribution/commercial task | Go/no-go evidence |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 4 | Stabilize a profitable service/asset line; isolate repeatable components. | Ask buyers for next recurring pain, not random features. | Quality and owner hours under control. |
| 5 | Pilot an unrelated niche using the same technical primitive where feasible. | Obtain at least one genuine paid opportunity, or retire. | New buyer pays for distinct value. |
| 6 | Add billing entitlement/reconciliation if recurring revenue exists. | Build a second acquisition source independent of one platform. | Measured conversion, collection and churn. |
| 7 | Formalize support categories and incident response; consider narrow contractor delegation. | Raise price only with measured willingness to pay and value. | Net contribution per owner hour improves. |
| 8 | Release one template/licensed product from repeated client work. | Use truthful demos, approved listings, consent-based referrals. | First independent paid download; support load viable. |
| 9 | Consider a read-only paid SaaS/monitor/API from three paid pilots. | Secure two explicit repeat-use signals. | Rights and ongoing margins verified. |
| 10 | Add a third revenue line only with enough capital, support, demand and legal clearance. | Expand into a new sector based on observable need. | Operations can sustain cancellations and outages. |
| 11 | Improve shared adapters, reporting, test coverage, cost controls. | Evaluate partnerships and renewal offers. | Failed acquisition channels turned off. |
| 12 | Annual portfolio audit; prune weak products; review customer concentration. | Decide whether a fourth line is actually justified. | Positive economic performance or a documented profitable growth path. |

**Expansion after the first year:** quarterly re-score the entire atlas; sample under-covered categories; replicate validated workflows to new sectors only after local buyer validation; add paid infrastructure only when cheaper than manual work; preserve cash for support, taxes, security and refunds. If owner time rises proportionally with customers, the line is a service firm—not passive income—and staffing/unit economics must say so.

### The throughput truth: how many opportunities can reasonably be tested?

At **two meaningful paid-offer experiments per week**, 52 weeks permits roughly **104 first-pass offer experiments**, before vacations, client commitments and failures. That is not 1,296 completed launches. A rapid automated *desk screen* can examine all 1,296; running genuine customer tests and safely operating them takes time. The correct target is **broad automated search + aggressive experiments + selective repeated launches**, not fictitious simultaneous rollouts. If evidence later supports a reusable customer-acquisition engine, increase experiment throughput; do not assume that engine exists today.

## 7. Operating limits and budget plans

### Work and capital limits

- **Time:** default 20 hours/week until an explicit schedule differs; keep a visible WIP queue. Weekly support incidents can override experiments.
- **Budget:** test $0 / $100 / $500 / $2,000 starting capital independently. Do not blend those cases and do not spend a hypothetical reserve.
- **Unspent capital:** remains cash, not operating profit. **Tax reserve:** excluded from discretionary launch money. **Unsettled sales:** not spendable cash.
- **Customer liabilities:** payment acceptance creates delivery, refund, privacy, support and record-retention obligations; budget for them *before* another launch.

| Initial discretionary budget | Practical first-week spending policy | Holdback discipline |
|---:|---|---|
| $0 | Use existing tools and lawful no-cost channels, local synthetic demos, a permitted marketplace where no required up-front fee applies. | If mandatory registration/account onboarding costs exist, pause—not debt or hidden cost. |
| $100 | Up to $20 necessary domain/transport, $20 exact-scope software, $20 relevant acquisition, $40 buffer. | Avoid a paid SaaS stack and unverified ads. |
| $500 | Up to $60 basic setup, $75 necessary tools, $100 bounded acquisition tests, $100 professional/compliance contingency, **$165 buffer**. | Release costs by paid evidence; do not empty the $500 account. |
| $2,000 | Up to $125 infrastructure/identity setup, $200 specialized tools, $250 measured channel tests, $375 professional/security contingency, **$1,050 buffer**. | Preserve at least half until repeat purchases and reliable collection justify spending. |

These allocations are **proposed caps**, not exact quotes. They exclude owner wages, possible insurance, specialized registration and hardware. Correct them using actual location, processor, professional advice and approved provider charges. You may start with a larger budget without changing the initial offer-selection gate.

### Committed recurring expense ceiling

Before any subscription or always-on worker, document: monthly base charge, per-use cap, FX exposure, worst-case abuse bill, cancellation method, payout lag, expected customer volume, who handles incidents, and the maximum loss if revenue remains **zero**. Any recurring plan lacking a firm cost limit is blocked. Default to batch/manual work until actual paid demand exists.

### Capacity planning formula

`Available monthly fulfillment hours = planned owner hours – sales hours – admin hours – build hours – incident reserve`.

`Max new paid pilots = floor(available fulfillment hours / measured p90 delivery hours)`, reduced for due-date clustering and skill constraints. Do not fill this number to 100%; retain capacity for rework and late customer inputs. Require a fresh estimate when a new vertical introduces unfamiliar requirements or a professional reviewer.

## 8. Reusable offer, pilot, acceptance, and contract templates

### One-page buyer-specific offer (complete before contacting anyone)

1. **Offer ID and segment:** exact `EXP-/FAST-/REPO-` record; buyer's function, company size, and a real task in its workflow.
2. **Observed problem:** what the buyer currently does, how often, existing software, error risk, and where time/money leaks. Mark unverified details as questions.
3. **Promise:** one observable result (e.g., “a reconciled inventory-exception CSV with zero unexplained record losses”). Avoid invented percentages or claims of prior client success.
4. **Inputs:** list, format, permission, redaction, retention, file limit, and acceptance of unsupported types.
5. **Output:** file/tool/action, versions, expected columns, access controls and the acceptance test.
6. **Price:** fixed CAD pilot price or written proposal; time cap, payment milestone, taxes if applicable and extra-work rate.
7. **Delivery:** begin only after agreed sample, legal approval and funded milestone; define realistic business-day turnaround, not “instant” by default.
8. **Scope exclusions:** compliance certification, irreversible live writes, custom integrations not agreed, unlimited revisions, unsupported languages, personal-data enrichment, and 24/7 human support.
9. **Privacy/security:** approved transfer and storage, who can access, planned deletion, backup treatment, incident contact and applicable terms.
10. **Fixes and refunds:** one agreed correction for a verified defect; material changes need a new scope. Refund/remedy terms must follow contract, law and provider policy.
11. **Differentiation:** why a buyer should pay instead of using an existing spreadsheet, software subscription, professional, or free script; verify with the buyer.
12. **Proof method:** synthetic/sample screenshots, real test log, and attribution. **Never** present demonstrations as client outcomes.

### Buyer discovery script, paraphrase naturally

- “Which exact report, import, reminder, approval, or creative task costs you time each week?”
- “What do you currently use? What works, and what fails?”
- “Can you provide a small redacted example or a self-contained spec? Please do not send sensitive data until we agree a secure process.”
- “Who approves paying for a fix? Is this urgent enough to fund a bounded pilot now?”
- “What result would you check to confirm delivery is correct? What would make this not worth the price?”
- “Would a repeat service, a one-time download, or a local-only tool fit better?”

### Acceptance specification example

**Task:** normalize a supplier CSV into a target SKU import schema.  
**Input:** one approved redacted example + signed field mapping; maximum 1,000 rows in the pilot.  
**Output:** input-preserving error manifest and validated target CSV; deterministic record totals and duplicate handling.  
**Pass:** required headers present; no unexplained deleted/duplicated IDs; clear report for unparseable values; no live store changes.  
**Fail:** unsupported formats, missing authorization or metrics unable to reconcile.  
**Commercial conditions:** price, payment milestone, turnaround from approved input, one revision, refund/remedy and data deletion agreed in writing.

A successful pilot requires **written acceptance or objective proof of acceptance criteria**, not a payment receipt alone.

## 9. Customer acquisition and evidence gathering

**Acquisition is part of the product.** No system is “passive” if it needs five owner hours of cold prospecting to sell a $19 download. Track every channel independently and calculate customer acquisition cost including owner time.

### Channels in priority order for a no-audience solo operator

1. **Explicit active requests:** locate real buyers asking to solve the exact problem on authorized freelance/project marketplaces or in permissioned professional communities. Evaluate the request's recency, budget, scope and the seller's eligibility. A listing is not a contract; avoid broad bids.
2. **Permissioned introductions and existing relationships:** ask whether a relevant problem actually exists. Permission for conversation is not unlimited marketing consent.
3. **Agency/consultant partnerships:** web agencies, operations consultants and bookkeepers may have repeated tasks within their *authorized scope*. Offer a clearly priced and reviewable pilot; comply with professional referral restrictions.
4. **Specialized marketplaces for a finished product:** asset marketplaces, template stores, code marketplaces and app stores can process discovery and fulfillment but impose listing, copyright, payout, fee, and support rules. Confirm seller eligibility and terms.
5. **Existing customer cross-sell:** ask which related problem is still unsolved. Get a specific paid opt-in; never silently enroll a service buyer in a subscription.
6. **Useful public demonstrations:** publish one real worked example with synthetic or rights-cleared material; publish only on channels allowing relevant content. Show how it compares to current substitutes.
7. **Opt-in list/newsletter:** explicit subscription, identification, unsubscribes and data minimization. Helpful for genuine repeat buyers—not purchased lists.
8. **Search-oriented guides and directories:** later-stage acquisition, built around original useful information. No scaled doorway pages, manufactured testimonials, ranking manipulation, or scraping.
9. **App ecosystems and integration partners:** a customer/partner must authorize access; platform approval, OAuth scopes and billing rules apply. Prefer one client-approved integration before a public app listing.
10. **Paid acquisition:** only after observed first-order contribution, verified conversion measurement, actual refund rate and capped downside. Test a narrow hypothesis, not “boost brand awareness.”

### Qualified-opportunity scoring

A prospective sale qualifies when (a) the problem is stated by the buyer, (b) they appear authorized to buy, (c) the scope is deliverable by you legally, (d) sample/privacy needs can be met, and (e) price is at least plausible. A random scraped email address is **not** a qualified lead. Record source URL, request date, buyer role, competing options and legal contact basis; remove/expire records appropriately.

### Outreach experiment protocol

- Choose one issue, one buyer class, and one permitted channel. Draft five truly relevant replies, each tied to an observable task and a truthful demonstration.
- Quote a narrow result with clear acceptance, not a general “AI automation for everything.”
- Track viewed request → permissible contact → reply → qualified conversation → proposal → paid funded milestone → accepted delivery → cash payout.
- Compare the *same* funnel across industries rather than reporting “ten DMs in plumbing” versus “ten downloads in game assets” as equal progress.
- If no reply, assess channel fit and specificity first. If replies but no sales, analyze trust, price, substitute, perceived value, scope and timing. If sales but losses, tighten delivery or stop.
- Follow up only under channel rules and the applicable law; do not use automatically generated outreach at scale without review and required consent.

### Partnership diligence

Define who contracts with the end customer, who owns the output, revenue share, renewal terms, data-controller/processor responsibilities, liability, refund authority, cancellation and no-poaching terms where enforceable. A “partner” who only promises future introductions is not validation. Pilot the arrangement with one paid customer before sharing credentials or making exclusive commitments.

## 10. Unit economics and financial reality

### Required equations (maintain separately for each opportunity ID)

- `EarnedRevenue = units delivered/accepted × realized price + earned subscription usage – discounts – recognized refunds`.
- `Contribution = earned revenue – card/marketplace/payout/FX fees – per-unit compute/material/contractor costs – attributable support/refund allowances – paid acquisition cost`.
- `OperatingProfit = total earned revenue – all operating cash expenses`; owner pay and personal income taxes are disclosed separately.
- `EconomicProfit = OperatingProfit – (all owner work hours × owner opportunity-cost rate)`.
- `MRR = sum(active paid recurring contracted monthly charges)`; not lifetime license sales, one-time setup charges, free users, or prepaid annual cash counted 12 times.
- `NetRevenueRetention = (opening cohort MRR + expansion – contraction – churn) / opening cohort MRR` where the opening cohort has paying customers; otherwise N/A.
- `GrossProfitPerHumanHour = actual attributable contribution / (research + selling + build + delivery + onboarding + support + admin hours)`.
- `CAC = (paid acquisition spend + sales contractor costs + appropriately valued sales owner time) / new paying customers`; undefined if no sales.
- `SimplePaybackMonths = CAC / monthly recurring contribution per retained customer` for recurring products, interpreted cautiously with churn, capital constraints and cohort timing.

**No assumed base-case volume is a guarantee.** If you have zero orders, profit may be negative from subscriptions and sunk work. If one customer prepays but processor settlement is delayed, booked revenue and available cash diverge. Taxes on money collected for a government are not revenue. A 30% income-tax cash reserve is only a liquidity placeholder, not a legal tax rate.

### Conditional cross-model examples already in the repository

The atlas uses *illustrative*, not observed, unit cases. For example: a `$499` fixed-scope service with **three sold units/month** can produce about **$1,218 conditional operating profit** under the atlas's fee, refund, variable and fixed cost assumptions; with zero sales, the model loses its fixed costs. A `$39` self-service product with **20 paid units/month** gives about **$605 conditional operating profit** under a different cost structure; it requires actual paying traffic. Neither figure pays the owner for acquisition or build time. Do not multiply these examples by 197 sectors and announce a portfolio forecast.

### Pricing approach

First price to deliver a credible bounded outcome and pay for the work. A low-priced “entry offer” is useful only if it produces positive contribution and a legitimate learning signal. For digital products, transaction fees and support minutes can consume much of $9–$19 price points. For B2B services, calculate acquisition cost using actual proposal/rejection hours. For subscriptions, charge for ongoing measurable service, include volume caps and unambiguous cancellation. For usage APIs, meter actual compute/network/extraction usage and impose quotas before opening checkout.

### Example conservative finance check before selling a $499 pilot

Assume only for illustration: realized CAD499 price; card + FX + marketplace blended allowance CAD45; variable tools CAD15; refund/rework allowance CAD20; 4 delivery hours and 2 sales/admin hours at a chosen CAD30/hour. Then cash contribution before fixed costs is `499 - 45 - 15 - 20 = CAD419`, while time-adjusted contribution is `419 - 6×30 = CAD239`. If that buyer instead costs 15 hours to acquire, time-adjusted contribution drops sharply. The correct price therefore depends on the **full funnel**, not the automation percentage of the final script. The assumptions must be replaced by actual expenses.

### Revenue, cash, and taxes stay separate

`Available cash = bank/processor settled funds – committed bills – customer/refund contingency – designated tax reserve – minimum operating buffer`. Reconcile provider payouts to *underlying transactions*, not as additional revenue. Never move client funds into personal purchases before known liabilities. Review provincial/federal registration and GST/HST thresholds across *all* your business activities; a new website does not create a fresh small-supplier allowance.

Before using it, search current real buyer requests, compare substitutions, check rights/competence and replace weak entries. The first three should come from distinct sectors with credible access. Do not select by convenience of writing code or familiarity with games.
